segments.name: The Name Changed at the Door

stops.name: Smyrna, the grandfather's counter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia's article on Jamie Dimon states outright that the paternal grandfather was a Greek immigrant banker who changed the family name from Papademetriou to Dimon, and names the parents Theodore Dimon and Themis Kalos; the Smyrna and Athens detail comes from family accounts reported in secondary profiles and no contemporaneous document for it was found. The date 1921 orders the segment only, set just ahead of the city's destruction the following year. Jamie Dimon himself never lived here.
stops.campa: Before there is a Dimon there is a Papademetriou, a Greek keeping bank accounts in Smyrna and in Athens, in a port where money moves between four languages and nobody is certain which empire will collect the tax. He crosses to the United States and shortens the name at the door, the way the century shortens names. Three generations of the family work in finance after him: the grandfather, then a stockbroker son named Theodore, then twin grandsons born in New York, one of whom will run the largest bank in America.
suggested_refs: The 1922 destruction of Smyrna, which ends the Greek commercial city the family banked in
sources: Wikipedia, 'Jamie Dimon' (fetched Aug 2026): Greek immigrant grandfather, name change from Papademetriou, parents Theodore Dimon and Themis Kalos

stops.name: Jackson Heights, born to the third generation
stops.date_confidence: birth date attested. Coordinates are neighborhood-level and not building-precise: Wikipedia's page for Public School 69 in Jackson Heights returned a 404 this pass, so the school's own address could not be confirmed.
stops.campa: James Dimon is born in New York City on the thirteenth of March, a son of Theodore Dimon, stockbroker, and Themis Kalos. His father and his grandfather sell securities for the same firm; nobody in that house needs the word commission explained. The early years are spent in Jackson Heights, Queens, and he attends Public School 69 there through roughly the fifth grade. Then the family moves into Manhattan. He has a twin brother, and the two of them are the third generation of the family to be raised around a brokerage.
suggested_refs: Public School 69, Jackson Heights, Queens
sources: Wikipedia, 'Jamie Dimon' (fetched Aug 2026)

stops.name: The Browning School, the Upper East Side
stops.date_confidence: graduation year 1974 attested; month defaulted to June and day to 01. Coordinates corrected this pass to the figures given by Wikipedia's article on the school, 40.764917 and -73.969222, replacing a research-pool value roughly 130 metres off. stops.campa: At 52 East 62nd Street, a private boys' school four blocks from Central Park, the son of a Queens stockbroker finishes his secondary education among the sons of the people his father's firm serves. He graduates in 1974. The distance from Public School 69 to Browning is about eight miles and the whole of an American social class, and he crosses it young enough that the second address becomes the native one. What he was like as a schoolboy is not recorded in anything reachable; the biographies set him down here and pick him up again at Tufts.

stops.name: Tufts, economics and psychology
stops.date_confidence: degree year attested by Wikipedia and by the official JPMorganChase biography; month defaulted to May for commencement and day to 01.
stops.campa: He reads economics and psychology at Tufts and takes the bachelor's degree summa cum laude in 1978, at twenty-two. Four decades of his working life will go on reading balance sheets and reading the men who present them, and both his admirers and his critics credit him with reading the second document faster. Medford sits twenty minutes from the Boston financial district, where his first job is already waiting for him. He does not leave the corridor between the two for another four years.

stops.name: Boston, the Management Analysis Center
stops.date_confidence: the two consulting years, 1978 to 1980, are attested; month and day are defaults. The firm's exact office address could not be established this pass, so the pin marks the Boston financial district generally and nothing narrower.
stops.campa: Before business school he works two years as a management consultant at Management Analysis Center, in the Boston financial district. It is the last position he will hold in which he advises rather than decides. The firm's exact address could not be established, so the pin marks the district and nothing narrower. What he did there, for which clients and in which industries, is not on the record either; the biographies pass over the two years in a clause. He enters Harvard Business School in 1980.

stops.name: Harvard Business School, Baker Scholar
stops.date_confidence: MBA year and Baker Scholar distinction attested by Wikipedia and by the official JPMorganChase biography; month defaulted to June for commencement. The marriage to Judith Kent is attested to May 1983 with no place given in any reachable source, so it is carried here in prose rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: He takes the MBA in 1982 and graduates a Baker Scholar, in the top five percent of the class. He meets Judith Kent here; they marry in May 1983. On graduating he goes to work as assistant to Sanford Weill at American Express, which is a choice of a man rather than of an institution. Weill will throw him out of it sixteen years later. In between he follows him from Manhattan to Baltimore, from Baltimore back to Wall Street, and from a consumer finance company into the largest financial company in the world.

stops.name: 125 Broad Street, assistant to Sandy Weill
stops.date_confidence: the 1982 start and the rise to vice president are attested; month and day are defaults. The 125 Broad Street address for American Express in these years is general knowledge and was not independently re-confirmed by fetch this pass, so the pin is flagged approximate.
stops.campa: He is twenty-six, assistant to the president of American Express, and he does the arithmetic Weill does not do himself: budgets, models, the numbers underneath a proposed acquisition. He is made a vice president. The building's address for these years is general knowledge rather than a thing confirmed by fetch this pass. Colleagues describe a young man with no patience for a briefing that has not been checked before it reaches him, a description that will follow him unchanged for forty years. He is in the building three years.

stops.name: 125 Broad Street, out with the man he came with
stops.date_confidence: the 1985 departure following Weill's ouster is attested; month and day are defaults chosen only to order the sequence.
stops.campa: Weill loses the internal contest at American Express and is pushed out. Dimon, twenty-nine, resigns and follows him into nothing in particular: no company, no title, an office and a search for something to buy. For most of a year the two of them are unemployed men with a subscription to the trade press, reading annual reports and telephoning boards. The loyalty is not sentimental. It is a bet that Weill will find something, and that being second inside it beats being tenth somewhere solvent.

stops.name: Baltimore, chief financial officer at thirty
stops.date_confidence: the 1986 appointment as chief financial officer of Commercial Credit at age thirty is attested; month and day are defaults. The exact office building could not be confirmed this pass, so the pin marks downtown Baltimore generally.
stops.campa: Weill finds it in Baltimore: Commercial Credit, a consumer finance company, unglamorous, undermanaged, and for sale. The pin marks downtown Baltimore, since the building itself could not be established. Dimon becomes its chief financial officer at thirty and later its president. The company lends small sums at high rates to people the money-centre banks do not serve, and it throws off cash. From this door, in a city neither man is from, everything after it is bought: Primerica, then Smith Barney, then Travelers, then Citicorp.

stops.name: Baltimore, a billion and a half for Primerica
stops.date_confidence: corrected this pass. The research pool dated the Primerica acquisition to 1987 on the strength of the JPMorganChase official biography; Wikipedia's article on Sanford I. stops.campa: Commercial Credit pays about $1.5 billion for Primerica, parent of Smith Barney, and takes the acquired company's name for its own. It is the first of the swallowings in which the smaller animal keeps the larger one's title. Dimon runs the integration, the part of a merger that nobody writes about, where two payrolls and two sets of accounts have to become one set by a Monday morning. In 1993 Primerica takes over the Travelers Corporation and changes its name again, and the group is on its third identity in six years.

stops.name: 399 Park Avenue, president of the largest company of its kind

stops.campa: Travelers Group and Citicorp announce a merger worth some seventy billion dollars, illegal on its face under the Glass-Steagall Act and legalised the following year by a Congress that rewrites the act to fit what has already happened. Dimon is named president of Citigroup, the largest financial company in the world. He does not get a chief executive title; Weill and John Reed take those, jointly. The two halves of the merged staff are still deciding whose people get which desk.

stops.name: Westchester County, asked to resign at the offsite
stops.date_confidence: corrected this pass and still soft. The research pool staged this at Citigroup's Manhattan headquarters on 1998-11-02; Wikipedia says only that 'Weill asked him to resign during a weekend executive retreat', which reporting places in Westchester on Sunday 1 November 1998. The retreat's actual site could not be sourced, so the coordinates are county-level placeholders for Westchester, not a venue, and the day is given as reconstruction. What is attested is the November 1998 removal and that it did not happen at 399 Park Avenue.
stops.campa: On a Sunday, at a Citigroup management retreat outside the city, Weill asks him to resign. The quarrel is over succession and over who governs which division of the merged firm; what was actually said in the room is thin in the record, and both men have given accounts of it since. He is forty-two. He leaves with no company and no title, and this time without Weill to follow. Sixteen years of attaching himself to one man end at a weekend offsite in Westchester, on a date the sources give as the first or the second of November.

stops.name: Chase Tower, Chicago, buying his own conviction
stops.date_confidence: the March 2000 appointment as chairman and chief executive of Bank One is attested; the day, 27 March, comes from the research pool's geography lens and is carried as reconstruction. The personal share purchase of about $56.75 million is attested in the same source set.
stops.campa: After sixteen months out of work he takes Bank One, the fifth-largest bank in the United States and the sickest of them, and moves to Chicago to run it. On the way in he buys about $56.75 million of its stock with his own money, which is the whole of the argument he intends to make to the staff and the shareholders, made once, in cash. The bank is losing money on credit cards and running a patchwork of unmerged computer systems from a dozen acquisitions. He cuts the dividend and starts consolidating the machines.

stops.date_confidence: completion date 1 July 2004 attested by the official JPMorganChase biography, along with the president and chief operating officer title.
stops.campa: Bank One and JPMorgan Chase complete their merger on the first of July 2004, and Dimon becomes president and chief operating officer of the combined bank, with the succession to the top job written into the agreement itself. stops.name: 33 Liberty Street, the Class A seat
stops.date_confidence: the election as a Class A director of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York is tagged R in the research pool: Wikipedia's Jamie Dimon article carries it but is self-contradictory about when, one section saying March 2008 and another the late 2010s, and Wikipedia's article on the Federal Reserve Bank of New York does not list him among directors at all. stops.campa: He is elected a Class A director of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, one of the seats the Federal Reserve Act reserves for representatives of the member banks. A commercial banker sits on the board of the institution that supervises him. The arrangement dates from 1913 and attracts almost no comment until 2008, when the same regional Fed becomes a counterparty on both sides of a rescue. The sources disagree about when his term began and how long it ran, and the Fed's own account does not name him among its directors.

stops.name: 383 Madison Avenue, two dollars a share
stops.date_confidence: corrected this pass. The research pool's geography lens carried a date range beginning 1998-03-16, a typographical error for 2008, and coordinates about 250 metres south of the building; the afterlife lens gave a third set of coordinates for the same tower and described 16 March as a closing date, which it is not. Wikipedia's Bear Stearns article gives the initial agreement 14 March 2008, the price revision 24 March, and shareholder approval 29 May. stops.campa: Bear Stearns cannot fund itself. Its counterparties stop rolling over the overnight repurchase agreements that the whole firm runs on, and inside a weekend the eighty-five-year-old house at 383 Madison Avenue is worth whatever somebody will pay before Monday. On the fourteenth of March JPMorgan agrees to buy it at two dollars a share, a price that values the tower above the business inside it. Bear's shareholders revolt. On the twenty-fourth the offer is raised to ten dollars, and they approve it on the twenty-ninth of May.
suggested_refs: 383 Madison Avenue, Bear Stearns headquarters, later JPMorgan's temporary headquarters during the rebuilding of 270 Park Avenue

stops.name: 33 Liberty Street, Maiden Lane
stops.date_confidence: the Maiden Lane structure and its figures are attested by Wikipedia's Bear Stearns article: a $29 billion first-priority loan from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York against a $30 billion pool of assets, with $1 billion subordinated from JPMorgan taking the first losses. The date is set to the 24 March revision, when the restructured terms were agreed.
stops.campa: The deal is not made without the state. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York lends $29 billion against a thirty-billion-dollar pool of Bear Stearns assets moved into a vehicle named Maiden Lane, after the street outside the building; JPMorgan puts in a billion of subordinated money that takes the first loss. Whatever is said afterward about the bank that rescued Wall Street, the arithmetic of this particular rescue is twenty-nine parts public to one part private, and the ratio is on the record from the first day.
suggested_refs: Maiden Lane LLC, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York vehicle created for the Bear Stearns assets

stops.name: Seattle, Washington Mutual closed on a Thursday
stops.date_confidence: date attested. Building corrected this pass: the research pool named WaMu Center as 1201 Third Avenue, but Wikipedia's article on the building states it stands at 1301 Second Avenue, on the opposite corner from 1201 Third Avenue, which was the earlier Washington Mutual Tower. stops.campa: The Office of Thrift Supervision closes Washington Mutual Bank on the twenty-fifth of September and hands it to the FDIC as receiver; within hours JPMorgan has bought the banking operations for $1.9 billion. It is the largest bank failure in American history and no depositor loses a cent. The purchase brings in the deposits, the branches and the banking assets of a company that had been among the largest mortgage lenders in the country. The Seattle headquarters at 1301 Second Avenue, built for WaMu two years earlier, will be renamed twice and end up carrying the buyer's name.

stops.name: The Treasury, the room nobody leaves
stops.date_confidence: the $25 billion of preferred stock and warrants issued to the Treasury under the Capital Purchase Program in October 2008 is attested; the day, 13 October, is the widely reported date of the meeting of the nine chief executives and is carried here as reconstruction, since Dimon's own physical presence in the building on that date was not independently confirmed this pass. Coordinates corrected from 38.8934 to 38.897556, about 465 metres: the pool's latitude fell near the Ellipse rather than on the Treasury Building.
stops.campa: In October the heads of the nine largest American banks are called to Washington and told, in one room, that all of them will take Treasury capital whether they need it or not, so that the ones who need it are not marked out by taking it. JPMorgan issues $25 billion of preferred stock and warrants under the Capital Purchase Program. The scheme is built so that accepting it will signal nothing about any particular bank. Dimon will spend the years afterward explaining that the money was pressed on him rather than asked for.

stops.name: 270 Park Avenue, the money given back
stops.date_confidence: June 2009 repayment attested by Wikipedia; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In June 2009 the bank repays the $25 billion, among the first of the nine to get out from under it. The Treasury keeps the warrants and sells them later at a profit, so the public is repaid with interest. From this point a sentence begins to circulate: that JPMorgan never needed saving and helped save everybody else. The sentence is true about the repayment and silent about Maiden Lane. Duff McDonald's biography of him is published the same year, and its title is Last Man Standing. Dimon does not invent the phrase, and he does not correct it.

stops.name: Washington, before the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the written statement was fetched as a PDF from the commission's own archive at fcic-static.law.stanford.edu and the quotation extracted verbatim from it. The specific hearing room could not be identified this pass, so the coordinates mark central Washington and nothing narrower.
stops.campa: He appears before the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission on the thirteenth of January 2010, seated with three other chief executives on the first day of its public hearings. The commission wants to know how the system was allowed to reach a point where its collapse had to be prevented at any price. His written statement concedes the premise and refuses the usual remedy: no institution, his own included, should be too big to fail, and the answer is not a cap on the size of banks but a way to let a very large one die without taking the economy down with it.
stops.quote: No institution, including our own, should be "too big to fail." The solution is not to cap the size of financial firms. We need a regulatory system that provides for even the biggest bank to be allowed to fail, but in a way that does not put taxpayers or the broader economy at risk.
stops.quote_source: Written testimony of Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, JPMorgan Chase & Co., before the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, 13 January 2010

stops.name: Washington, the argument with Mark Carney
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on venue. Wikipedia gives the date and the fact of a heated exchange with Mark Carney, then governor of the Bank of Canada, over the Basel III capital rules, but does not state where it happened; the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Washington is a reasonable placement and not a confirmed one.
stops.campa: He argues in public with Mark Carney, then governor of the Bank of Canada, over the Basel III capital rules. Dimon holds that the requirements are excessive and that they disadvantage American banks; Carney holds the line and does not soften it for the room. Where the exchange happened is a reconstruction and is not confirmed; only the date and the fact of the quarrel are attested. He does not lobby quietly. He argues from platforms, with the trade press listening and the regulator sitting three feet away.

stops.name: Canary Wharf, a tempest in a teapot
stops.date_confidence: the 13 April 2012 earnings-call remark is attested indirectly: Dimon's own 2012 shareholder letter quotes his 'tempest in a teapot' comment back and dates it, and the letter's text was extracted from the official PDF this pass. No transcript of the call itself was located. The Canary Wharf pin marks JPMorgan's London operations generally; the Chief Investment Office desk's exact floor was not confirmed. Losses eventually totalling about $6.2 billion, and the May 2012 disclosure, are attested by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: In the Chief Investment Office at Canary Wharf, an operation whose stated purpose is hedging the bank's own balance sheet, a trader named Bruno Iksil has built a credit derivatives position so large that the rest of the market can see it and nicknames him the London Whale. Reports appear in the press in early April. On the thirteenth Dimon calls the whole matter a tempest in a teapot on an earnings call. The position is not a hedge, and it does not stop losing. By the time it is closed out the loss runs to about $6.2 billion.
suggested_refs: The Chief Investment Office synthetic credit portfolio and the trader Bruno Iksil

stops.name: Davos, hedge funds are pretty opaque too
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the year. The exchange is widely quoted with this wording and attributed to the Financial Times; 2013 is the best-supported year and not a confirmed one, and this pass could not re-verify the session against a live source. The coordinates are inherited byte-identical from paul_singer.journey.json, where the same exchange is staged from the other side.
stops.campa: On a World Economic Forum panel he is needled from the floor by Paul Singer, who says the banks' published accounts are so opaque that no outsider can tell the sound ones from the quietly rotten. Dimon does not let it pass. With all due respect, he answers, hedge funds are pretty opaque too. The exchange is reported by the Financial Times and quoted back at both men for years.
